Title: A generic “preserve editorial intent” rule can fail — and can make outputs less faithful
Description: A single, generic Narrative prompt section intended to preserve Synthesis editorial hierarchy did not keep the primary message or audience scope intact; instead candidate runs systematically subordinated company identity, made orchestration the central positioning, and introduced unsupported assertions. The experiment shows that adding a generic editorial-hierarchy constraint is not a reliable way to preserve a specific synthesis intent.
Audience: Prompt engineers, Narrative authors, content-quality reviewers, and product leads responsible for model-driven content pipelines.
Rationale: Why it matters: Teams that treat a short, reusable editorial rule as a safety net risk subtle but repeatable editorial drift — shifting emphasis away from the intended company-level message toward technical exposition, and even adding unsupported audience or validation claims. This can undermine publishability and violate hard promotion gates. Gaps and uncertainty: the experiment used three runs per condition (not statistically significant), no explicit temperature/seed was set, and the provider alias may map to different backends; these factors limit how broadly the result can be generalized.
Evidence: Facts from the experiment: the candidate prompt added a generic section titled “Preserve Editorial Intent from the Synthesis.” Candidate Narrative mean score fell to 4.00/10 (baseline 6.00/10); Compose mean fell to 3.33/10 (baseline 5.67/10). All three candidate Narrative and Compose runs failed the orchestration-as-support gate (C) and introduced unsupported additions (D failed in every candidate run). The team’s decision: “Do not promote” and restore the production prompt byte-for-byte (rollback SHA-256 matches baseline).
